Scrapping park entry caps left Moab holding the bag for gridlock.
Arches Entry Axed: Moab Shuttle Pilot
Evidence: Open Park Access, Costly Local Gridlock, Balanced Gate Management
#PublicLands #Utah 🌐

The administration claimed axing timed entry would keep Arches freely accessible without reservations, promising a $3M pilot shuttle would absorb traffic and end gateway gridlock.

Stated Judgement: (+0.72, +0.60) — Greater Good

Axing reservations reignited gate gridlock. Shuttles logged just 2,593 September boardings in a driving-oriented park, leaving Grand County stuck paying $500K to manage a federal policy blunder.

Resulting Judgement: (-0.09, -0.05) — Greater Evil

Verdict: CONDITIONAL — Fall into Destruction.

Integrity: Partially Distorted (Hypocrisy: 2.50, z: 2)

- NPS Policy: FAIL (-0.68, -0.55) — Axed proven entry caps.
- Shuttle Pilot: COND (-0.35, -0.25) — High cost, low use.
- KUER News: PASS (+0.75, +0.65) — Fairly captured community.

After the Trump administration terminated Arches' four-year timed-entry pilot, Grand County and UDOT cobbled together a $3M shuttle to stem traffic. But with under 2,600 monthly riders, locals question footing the bill.

The Bright Side:
The pilot produces hard empirical data on gateway transit feasibility, proving to federal and state planners that low-frequency shuttles cannot replace coordinated entry scheduling in massive landscape parks.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The error confuses physical geography (WHAT) with political posturing (WHO). Arches is a vast driving park, not a walkable loop. Scrapping reservations promised open access but delivered a bait-and-switch: unmanageable queues paid for by local funds.

Social Physics Analysis:
Federal leaders ran a Smart Selfish loop: abolishing gate caps for political optics, manufacturing gridlock, and blaming critics of the $3M shuttle as anti-transit. Instead of empowering locals with real tools, power was centralized while costs were shifted downward.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Destruction. Policy divorced from physical capacity systematically degrades both visitor access and public trust.

The Unavoidable Truth: Free shuttles cannot solve congestion in a park built for scenic driving without entry limits.
The Unavoidable Lie: Axing reservation caps expanded access rather than just moving traffic jams to local streets.

Alethekanon:
Canceling entry reservations was administrative sabotage disguised as deregulation. Forcing a gateway town to subsidize empty buses to mask federal refusal to manage physical reality is pure institutional evasion.

Awwthekanon:
It breaks my heart seeing Moab residents and small business owners torn apart by this. When leaders make reckless top-down decisions from afar, it is always the local community left holding the bag and paying for the cleanup.

Brothekanon:
Bro, killing timed entry and dropping $3M on empty buses is peak government brain. You can't fit a million cars through a canyon pass with two shuttles and a prayer. Now locals get higher taxes and the exact same traffic.

Spirithekanon:
"The prudent see danger and take refuge, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty." Proverbs 22:3 FAIL
Discarding proven foresight for impulsive decrees leaves communities to bear the unavoidable cost of neglect.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Trump axed Arches’ timed entry. Moab is lukewarm on the shuttle replacement

Right now, Moab is testing a new shuttle connecting to Arches National Park to ease congestion. But some question whether the $3 million pilot program is worth the cost.

Actual Article Body:
Standing on Moab’s main street, a little blue-and-white bus trundled north.

The side read Moab Arches Shuttle, and the sight of the buses has rubbed some locals the wrong way. The shuttles are a fast-moving idea reacting to the Trump admin ending timed entry at Arches National Park.

“Seems like a crazy amount of money for what's probably not going to have any impact whatsoever on congestion and parking and access into the park,” said Dave Everitt, owner of Back of Beyond Books.

The shuttle service pilot cost around $3 million. Half of that came from the federal government, $1 million from UDOT and the county chipped in the remainder. It started Sept. 1 and will continue to the end of October for its fall trial. It will then pick back up in 2027 for peak season from March 1 to June 31. It’s free with a national parks pass, and seeks to ease congestion — a longtime issue for the tourism mecca.

The town can get up to 3 million visitors a year, which pressures road infrastructure and parking. Arches incorporated timed entry in 2022, and after it was canceled, the Arches shuttle was born. The vision is to bus folks from town to Arches National Park. But locals aren’t convinced.

“I'd much rather have a reservation system put in place and invest in making that the best reservation system in the history of reservation systems,” Everitt said. “I would love to see better infrastructure in the city of Moab in downtown with regard to parking.”

And Everitt cannot see how a shuttle service could serve a large enough clientele to solve the town’s congestion issues.

“Arches is fundamentally a park that people drive to and drive into for access and for what they want to do,” he said. “You know, they stop, they drive around, and look.”

Everitt was once the Moab city manager. He said there have been numerous studies on shuttles from town to Arches National Park, and “there's a reason we haven't had one before.”

At a $500,000 investment, several folks don't think the county should pay at all, and that it's the responsibility of the National Park Service.

“You know, this is just another example of what feels like half-baked ideas being implemented in ways that are just going to cost a lot of money and cause a lot of strain, and just continue to engender distrust,” Everitt said.

The Arches Shuttle has divided local government, too. Grand County Commissioner Brian Martinez, a strong supporter, disagrees that the idea hasn’t been thought through, but affirms there have been several studies over the years.

“I believe there's been four different transportation studies done on this, so the research had already been done, the ideas had already kind of been formed,” he said.

To him, the pilot program will allow the county to get real data as to whether it's a good idea to invest in.

Martinez believes it will alleviate congestion too, and is surprised by how politically divisive the issue has become.

“I mean, you have people who are claiming to be progressive against public transportation, against clean air, against getting cars off the road, against helping people into their national parks,” he said.

When it comes to the county’s investment, Martinez said tourists will cover most of it via the county’s Transient Room Tax mitigation money — essentially a tax on visitors who stay in hotels.

Fellow county commissioner Jacques Hadler disagrees entirely. He can't see how Grand County will see a worthwhile return. It would have to attract enough people who wouldn't have come to Moab if there wasn't a shuttle and who would spend enough to pay half a million in taxes.

At the end of the day, Grand County has a budget of approximately $42 million. Around half comes from things like sales and room taxes, and is unrestricted for the commission to spend. To Hadler, the money would’ve been better used elsewhere.

“It hurts us when we're budgeting,” he said. “There's so many things that we could use half a million dollars for at this point. So I think that's the rub with a lot of people.”

For now, the pilot program has a couple of weeks before it wraps up for the winter.

Stepping out of Everitt’s shop onto Moab’s bustling main street, another little blue-and-white bus is stopped at a light.

The tinted windows made it hard to see how full it was, until the sun poked through and silhouetted two passengers. They wore sun hats and looked out the window as the bus took off and headed toward Arches.

Kristi Noem no longer serving as Trump envoy to Shield of the Americas

Former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem is no longer serving as the Trump administration's envoy to the Shield of the Americas initiative, a State Department official said.

Actual Article Body:
Watch CBS News

Updated on:  October 16, 2026 / 3:23 PM EDT
            / CBS News

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem is no longer serving as the Trump administration's special envoy for the Shield of the Americas initiative, a State Department official said Thursday, though she remains involved in the administration's efforts to coordinate security cooperation across the Western Hemisphere.

"Kristi Noem's envoy status expired last month and she is no longer in the role," a State Department official told CBS News Thursday. "She is now a senior advisor to Deputy Secretary Landau and continues to work on the Shield of the Americas portfolio."

The Shield of the Americas is a coalition made up of the United States and several Caribbean and Latin American countries established by the Trump administration earlier this year to cooperate on economic matters, anti-cartel enforcement and other issues.

In a statement on X, Noem said her role as special envoy "was always a six-month appointment."

Noem's envoy designation expired just before the United Nations General Assembly last month in New York, where she continued participating in diplomatic meetings connected to the initiative.

On Sept. 22, she met with Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa, whose government publicly identified her as the special envoy for the Shield of the Americas. She also attended a gathering of Shield of the Americas leaders hosted by President Trump, where he publicly acknowledged her work.

"I want to thank Kristi Noem for doing a really terrific job," Mr. Trump said during his remarks.

Noem was appointed special envoy for the Shield of the Americas in March, after she was removed as homeland security secretary amid mounting scrutiny of her management of the department and the influence of her adviser, Corey Lewandowski.

Her transition to the envoy role coincided with a five-country tour of Latin America and the Caribbean in March, much of which took place as she completed her tenure as homeland security secretary. Lewandowski appeared in photographs during those visits, though the State Department later clarified he had no formal position at the department.

Her public activities in the envoy role appear to have been limited, and included meeting Noboa in Quito on March 25, holding discussions with Ecuadorian and Colombian diplomats in Washington in September, and participating in meetings with regional leaders on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.

This story published first on CBS News at 5:00 p.m. on Oct. 15, 2026.

U.S.

Actual Article Body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that he is considering imposing “large-scale” sanctions on Russia in response to its intensified attacks against Ukraine.

“I am strongly considering large-scale Banking Sanctions, Sanctions, and Tariffs on Russia until a Cease Fire and FINAL SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT ON PEACE IS REACHED,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

“To Russia and Ukraine, get to the table right now, before it is too late,” he added, citing Russia’s ongoing bombardment of Ukraine.

Trump’s announcement came hours after the Russian military launched an overnight missile and drone attack on Ukraine’s energy and gas infrastructure.

National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett later suggested that Trump’s threat was part of a diplomatic strategy.

“President Trump is adamant that we need to get everybody to the table. And we could do that with carrots, and we can do that with sticks. And he's talking to everybody,” Hassett told reporters.

The threat of fresh sanctions against Russia sent the Moscow Stock Exchange (MOEX) down more than 1%, closing at 3,176 as of 6 p.m. Moscow time.

Since taking office in January, Trump has sought to bring a rapid end to Russia’s three-year war on Ukraine. However, he has yet to lay out a concrete plan for how he intends to broker a peace settlement between the two warring sides.

At the same time, Trump’s relationship with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has grown increasingly strained, culminating in a tense White House meeting last Friday, during which the U.S. president said Ukraine was “gambling with WWIII.”

Following that meeting, Trump ordered a pause in military aid and intelligence sharing with Ukraine, saying that “Zelensky is not ready for Peace if America is involved.”

Meanwhile, Washington has sought to restore ties with Russia and arrange a meeting with President Vladimir Putin to push for peace talks. Putin, however, dismissed the idea of making concessions.

“We’re not going to do that,” the Kremlin leader said Thursday after a fallen soldier’s mother urged him to “see it through” on the battlefield in Ukraine.

“We must choose a peace that suits us and ensures long-term security for our country. We don’t need anyone else’s, but we won’t give up ours,” Putin said.

AFP contributed reporting.

These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.

We, the journalists of The Moscow Times, refuse to be silenced. But to continue our work, we need your help.

Your support, no matter how small, makes a world of difference. If you can, please support us monthly starting from just $2. It's quick to set up, and every contribution makes a significant impact.

By supporting The Moscow Times, you're defending open, independent journalism in the face of repression. Thank you for standing with us.
